newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus protest turns violent, dozens arrested.
newsitem.headline: Belarus protest turns violent, dozens arrested.

text.p: Nationalists hurled chunks of ice, smashed police car windows and yelled "Long live Belarus" on Sunday as police used truncheons and tear gas to quell their protests against President Alexander Lukashenko's pro-Moscow policies.
There were injuries on both sides as the latest in a string of unsanctioned protests against Lukashenko's increasingly authoritarian rule turned violent.
Riot helmets flew through the air and a policeman was seen clutching his bloody nose after about 4,000 people ignored a ban on marching to a sanctioned rally on Yakob Kolas Square.
One woman protester nursed two black eyes as fights broke out on the edge of the rally, attended by about 10,000 people.
Interfax news agency reported that Serzh Alexandrov, first secretary at the U.S. embassy which has often criticised Lukashenko, was one of 70 people arrested.
The agency added that police had heard from "competent sources" that Alexandrov, an ethnic Belarussian, was working for the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency).
An officer of the embassy's security body told Reuters he could confirm that Alexandrov had been detained, but Janet Demery, the embassy's official spokeswoman, said she could not.
She said Western diplomats often watched opposition protests in Belarus from the sidelines "as part of a brief to observe the politicial situation, but not to participate".
Two liberal politicians, Gennady Karpenko who heads the Civic Union party and his colleague Yuri Zakharenko, a former interior minister, were also detained briefly.
Dozens of arrests were made as nationalists from the Popular Front marched at the unsanctioned part of the protest, where most of the violence occurred.
Interfax said two of three injured policemen were taken to hospital, where one of them was operated on for head injuries.
Karpenko is one of the leading figures in the official opposition to Lukashenko, who disbanded parliament last November after a landslide win at a referendum gave him sweeping powers.
Police have detained scores of anti-Lukashenko protesters in recent weeks, though most have been released within a few days.
"How can we talk about democracy when people are being put in prison just because they want to express a different point of view?" Semyon Sharetsky asked the crowd on Yakob Kolas Square.
Sharetsky was head of the old parliament and led attempts to stop Lukashenko holding the referendum, denounced as illegitimate by Western officials.
The nationalists object strongly to Lukashenko's building closer ties with Moscow, a policy which nevertheless has the backing of most of the population of 10 million.
The 42-year-old former farm boss is opposed by a loose union of prominent politicians, nationalists, intellectuals and students mostly in the capital.

The nationalists, shouting "Belarus into NATO" and "We will not sell our nation's glory" and waving red-and-white flags replaced under Lukashenko by Soviet emblems, were marking the anniversary of an independent republic created in 1918.
The republic lasted only a few months until it was incorporated by Russian Bolsheviks and Belarus stayed under Moscow rule until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

Sunday's was the latest in a string of protests against Lukashenko, who has cracked down on opposition forces by restricting rallies, arresting protesters and putting a senior opposition leader in prison for five days in recent weeks.
The United States this week cut off $40 million in aid to Belarus because of its human rights performance.
